StrategyGrowthDistributionRevenue

Build it to run without you

By lowob · 27 March 2026 · 4-minute read · Strategy

A GTM system is only an asset if the company owns it: the accounts, the records, the routines and the reasons. Build for handover from day one, then score yourself across all ten parts of this series and fix the weakest link first.

What "owning it" means

Asset What to own Common failure
Accounts Ad, social, email, analytics, domain, community admin rights, all in the company's name Agency or ex-employee holds the logins
Records Evidence log, investor pipeline, partner list, customer source data Spread across personal inboxes and DMs
Routines Runbooks for recurring work: investor update, partner launch, community ritual, monthly report Only one person knows how it's done
Reasons Why each major decision was made and what was rejected The next hire repeats an experiment that already failed

The last row is the one almost nobody keeps, and the one that saves the most money. A decision record of three lines — what we chose, what we rejected, what would change our minds — is enough.

If you bring in outside help

Write handover into the scope at the start, not the end. Accounts opened in your name. Reports in a format your team can produce without the agency. A final session that walks your team through every runbook. A good partner should be trying to make themselves unnecessary for the work they've finished.

The ten-question self-score

Score each question 0–5. Zero means "not at all"; five means "done, with evidence I could show an investor today."

# Question Part
1 Do fundraising, community and customer work run off one calendar with one owner? 1
2 Is there a one-sentence product truth, and a belief statement per audience? 2
3 Is there a dated evidence log with incentivised and organic activity separated? 3
4 Is the raise run from a researched list, tracked like a pipeline? 4
5 Does the community have a named job, measured by contribution? 5
6 Can you name the first hundred people who'd notice if you disappeared? 6
7 Do you have design partners with written success tests and agreed post-pilot prices? 7
8 Is every channel sorted open, restricted or closed, with partners ahead of paid media? 8
9 Do you report activation, retention, revenue, efficiency and source, instead of reach? 9
10 Would the system keep running if your most important person left tomorrow? 10

Reading your score (a rule of thumb, not a verdict):

40–50: the system is in place. Spend on scale.

30–39: it works, with gaps. Fix the two lowest scores before the next big spend.

Under 30: you're likely spending on step eight with steps two and three unanswered. Go back to the lowest-numbered question you scored below 3 and start there.

A zero on question 2, 3 or 7 is a stop sign regardless of total: no clear truth, no evidence or no real customer means the next dollar of fundraising or marketing is guesswork.

For teams launching a token, this sits alongside a stricter launch-readiness check covering legal, security, treasury and liquidity, which deserves its own piece.

Closing the spine

The order matters more than any single tactic in these ten parts. Name the buyer. Write one truth. Collect evidence. Raise against it. Give your community a job. Make your first customers partners. Distribute through people who already have your buyer's trust. Measure what comes back. Then make sure you own all of it.

That's the whole system. Most teams have pieces of it. Very few have it in order.

The checklist

Every account in the company's name, with an access list.

Evidence log, pipeline and monthly report in shared, owned tools.

Runbooks for the five most repeated GTM tasks.

A decision record for every major choice.

Handover written into every outside scope.

The ten-question self-score, done and dated.

If you'd like a second pair of eyes on your score, bring us the commercial problem.

lowob takeaways

  • Every ad, social, email, analytics, domain and community admin account should be in the company's name.
  • Write handover into an outside partner's scope at the start, not the end.
  • A zero on product truth, evidence or real customers is a stop sign regardless of the total score.
